rules.title: Ban on using or distributing a common pricing algorithm to restrain trade or coerce adoption of recommended prices
rules.requirement: In California it is unlawful for a landlord or software vendor to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm (software used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend or set prices or terms) as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce others into adopting its recommended price or terms. If you suspect coordinated algorithmic rent-setting, you can report it to the Attorney General or consult a lawyer about antitrust remedies.

coverage_conditions.summary: Applies statewide to any person who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm; covers all rental units in California (and other products and services).

rules.exemptions: "Person" does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (AB 325, Stats. 2025, Ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.source_type: official text captured by the team (not in the starter pack)

rules.title: Ban on using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade
rules.requirement: Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

coverage_conditions.summary: Applies statewide to any person (including landlords and software vendors) who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm; not limited to particular buildings. End consumers are excluded from the definition of person.

rules.exemptions: "Person" does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729(a) (AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.penalty: Violation of the Cartwright Act, which is punishable as a crime; general Cartwright Act enforcement applies.

rules.title: Ban on coercing adoption of prices or terms recommended by a common pricing algorithm
rules.requirement: It is illegal for anyone using or distributing a shared pricing algorithm to coerce another person to adopt the price or commercial terms (such as availability or level of service) it recommends. This can cover pressure to adopt software-recommended rents.

coverage_conditions.summary: Applies statewide to any person who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm and coerces another to adopt its recommended price or commercial term; not limited to particular buildings.

rules.exemptions: "Person" does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
rules.citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729(b) (AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
rules.quoted_span: (b) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm if the person coerces another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by the common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in the jurisdiction of this state.
rules.penalty: Violation of the Cartwright Act, which is punishable as a crime.

rules.title: Tenant screening fee cap, receipts and refunds (Civil Code 1950.6)
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge you at most $68.96 in 2026 to screen your application, must give you a receipt, an itemized cost list, a copy of any credit report, and a refund of any unused part of the fee. The landlord cannot charge a fee if no unit is available, and must refund the fee if you are not selected unless it uses a first-qualified-applicant policy and charges only applicants it considers.
rules.key_value: $68.96 maximum screening fee (2026)

coverage_conditions.summary: All residential rental applicants statewide, including in Berkeley.

rules.interaction: Berkeley BMC 13.78.010 requires landlords to disclose this state-law cap and fee rights to applicants.
rules.quoted_span: The landlord must also return a screening fee to any applicant not selected, or have a policy under which they: (1) review applications in the order received and the first qualified applicant gets the unit, and (2) do not charge a screening fee to any applicant not considered.
rules.consolidation_note: Fields filled from D026, which state the same law.

rules.title: Conditions for charging a screening fee; refunds
rules.requirement: A landlord cannot charge a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or soon. To charge a fee, the landlord must either consider applications first-come in writing-disclosed order, charging only when your application is actually considered, or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days after you applied, whichever comes first.
rules.key_value: Full refund within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever comes first (or first-come process)

coverage_conditions.summary: All residential rental property in California; applies to applicants and to guarantors or cosigners.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Does not preempt deposit and fee rules of federal or state housing assistance programs

rules.exemptions: Under the first-come option, no refund is required for an applicant denied after consideration for failing the screening criteria. Inadvertent fees from concurrent applications must be refunded within 7 days, or applied to another unit at the applicant's choice.
rules.quoted_span: An application screening process in which the landlord or their agent returns the entire screening fee to any applicant who is not selected for tenancy, regardless of the reason, within 7 days of selecting an applicant for tenancy or 30 days of when the application was submitted, whichever occurs first.

rules.title: Screening fee receipt and credit report copy
rules.requirement: The landlord must give you a receipt itemizing the out-of-pocket costs and time spent screening you, delivered in person, by mail, or by email if you agree. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days of receiving it.
rules.key_value: Itemized receipt; credit report copy within 7 days

coverage_conditions.summary: All residential rental property in California; applies to applicants and to guarantors or cosigners.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Does not preempt deposit and fee rules of federal or state housing assistance programs

rules.quoted_span: The landlord or their agent shall provide, personally, or by mail, the applicant with a receipt for the fee paid by the applicant, which receipt shall itemize the out-of-pocket expenses and time spent by the landlord or their agent to obtain and process the information about the applicant.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act statewide just cause eviction requirement
rules.requirement: Once you have lawfully lived in your unit for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added, all tenants for 12 months or one tenant for 24 months), your landlord can only end your tenancy for a just cause listed in the law and must state it in the written notice. For no-fault evictions, such as owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, or substantial remodel, the landlord must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your final month's rent; otherwise the notice is void.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months of tenancy; no-fault relocation of 1 month's rent

coverage_conditions.summary: Covers most residential rental property in California after 12 months of tenancy. Exempt: housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years; owner-occupied duplexes; owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than two units or bedrooms; units where the tenant shares a kitchen or bath with a resident owner; separately alienable single-family homes or condos not owned by a REIT, corporation or corporate-member LLC, if proper notice was given; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotels, dorms and care facilities. Does not apply where a qualifying local just cause ordinance governs the unit.

Deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing
Homeowner of a mobilehome

rules.exemptions: Hotels; care facilities; school dorms; units sharing a kitchen or bath with a resident owner; owner-occupied single-family homes renting up to two units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplexes (neither unit an ADU); housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable property not owned by a REIT, corporation or corporate-member LLC, with written notice; deed-restricted affordable housing; property covered by a qualifying local just cause ordinance.
rules.interaction: Does not apply to property covered by a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before Sept. 1, 2019, or to a later-adopted or amended local ordinance that is more protective (with a binding local finding); in those cases the local ordinance applies. A property cannot be subject to both. A local ordinance adopted after Sept. 1, 2019 that is less protective cannot be enforced unless this section is repealed.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2 (as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203 (AB 1529))
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.conflict_note: Two dates appear: subdivision (m) says the section became operative April 1, 2024, while the history note says the current amendment (AB 1529) took effect January 1, 2026. The section is repealed as of January 1, 2030. The state law also overrides less protective local ordinances adopted after Sept. 1, 2019.
rules.penalty: Notice void for noncompliance. For material violation: actual damages, discretionary attorney's fees and costs, up to three times actual damages plus punitive damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct. The Attorney General, city attorney or county counsel may seek injunctive relief.

rules.title: Housing Crisis Act relocation for lower-income households displaced by demolition for new construction
rules.requirement: If you are a lower-income household (80% AMI or lower) displaced because your protected unit is demolished and replaced with new construction, you are entitled to relocation benefits equal to those public agencies must pay under Gov. Code § 7260 et seq.
rules.key_value: Relocation consistent with Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. public-entity relocation benefits

coverage_conditions.summary: Lower-income households (80% AMI or lower) displaced by demolition of protected units for new construction.
required_facts_not_in_data: Whether the unit is a protected unit being demolished for new construction
Tenant household income (80% AMI or lower)

rules.interaction: In Los Angeles, owners pay the higher of the HCA or City (RSO/JCO/RPO) amounts. The RSO/JCO amounts must be enhanced for lower-income tenants under the HCA even where the RPO does not apply.
rules.citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 66300.6(b)(4)(A) (Housing Crisis Act of 2019, SB 330, as amended by SB 8 and AB 1218)
rules.quoted_span:
The City’s Resident Protections Ordinance (RPO) and the
State’s Housing Crisis Act (HCA) require that ONLY lower income households (80%  AMI or
lower) being displaced for demolition of their units where the owner will replace the units
with new construction receive relocation payment consistent to the relocation benefits
required to be paid by public entities under Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 7260) of
Division 7 of Title 1 (Government Code 66300.6(b)(4)(A)).

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482) statewide rent cap
rules.requirement: If your unit is more than 15 years old and not under local rent control, your annual rent increase is capped at 5% plus the regional cost-of-living change, or 10%, whichever is lower. Units already covered by Los Angeles's RSO follow the RSO instead.
rules.key_value: lesser of 5% + CPI or 10%

coverage_conditions.summary: Residential units more than 15 years old (rolling), excluding units already subject to local rent control (LA RSO) and other listed exemptions.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: deed-restricted affordable housing
certain dormitories
single-family homes and condominiums not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, where the tenant was given written notice

rules.exemptions: Units built within the last 15 years (rolling); deed-restricted affordable units; certain dormitories; two-unit properties where the owner occupied the other unit for the entire tenancy; qualifying single-family homes and condos with written notice; units already subject to the RSO.
rules.interaction: Units already subject to the City's RSO are not covered by AB 1482.
rules.quoted_span: rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region in which the property is located, or 10% whichever is lower

rules.title: Statewide rent increase cap (Tenant Protection Act)
rules.requirement: Within any 12-month period, your landlord may not raise your rent by more than 5% plus the local CPI change, or 10%, whichever is lower, and may raise it in no more than two steps. The base is the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months, ignoring discounts. If you have been overcharged, you can sue for the excess, and for up to three times the excess if the landlord acted willfully.
rules.key_value: lesser of 5% + CPI or 10% per 12 months

coverage_conditions.summary: Most residential rental units in California. Exempt: housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); units covered by stricter local rent control; owner-occupied duplexes; deed-restricted affordable or subsidized housing; school dormitories; and separately alienable homes or condos not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, if the tenant received the required written notice.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing
Dormitories owned by higher-education institutions or K-12 schools
Separately alienable single-family homes or condos not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, where the tenant received written exemption notice
Homeowners of mobilehomes (Section 798.9)

rules.exemptions: Affordable deed-restricted or subsidized housing; school dormitories; housing under stricter local rent control; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); separately alienable homes or condos not owned by a REIT, corporation, or LLC with a corporate member, with the required notice; owner-occupied two-unit properties (neither unit an ADU or JADU); mobilehome homeowners. A new tenancy may set the initial rent freely.
rules.interaction: Does not apply to housing subject to local rent control (consistent with Costa-Hawkins, Civ. Code § 1954.50 et seq.) that restricts annual increases to less than the state cap. The section does not expand or limit local authority to regulate rents.
rules.quoted_span: Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
rules.conflict_note: The operative text (subd. (n)) says the section became operative April 1, 2024; the history note says it was effective January 1, 2024. Subdivision (h) also applies the cap to increases on or after March 15, 2019 (February 18, 2021 for mobilehomes). The section sunsets January 1, 2030.
rules.penalty: Civil action for injunctive relief, damages equal to the overcharge, and discretionary attorney's fees. Up to treble damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious conduct. Enforceable by the Attorney General and city attorneys or county counsel. Three-year limitations period. Waivers are void.

rules.title: Source-of-income discrimination ban in housing
rules.requirement: A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources.

coverage_conditions.summary: Owners of any housing accommodation in California.

rules.exemptions: Asking in writing or orally about the level or source of income is not by itself source-of-income discrimination.
rules.quoted_span: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.

rules.title: Income standard must be based on tenant's portion of rent for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent.
rules.key_value: income standard based on tenant's portion of rent

coverage_conditions.summary: Rental housing in California where the applicant has a government rent subsidy.

rules.exemptions: Owners may still verify employment, request landlord references, and verify identity.

rules.title: Alternative to credit history for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history.

coverage_conditions.summary: Rental housing in California where the applicant has a government rent subsidy.

rules.title: Source-of-income discrimination prohibited in rental housing (FEHA)
rules.requirement: A California landlord cannot refuse to rent to you, or give you different terms such as a higher deposit, because of how you pay rent, including a Section 8 voucher or other rental assistance. If this happens, you can file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department within one year or sue in court within two years.

coverage_conditions.summary: Applies to most housing accommodations in California and to most housing providers, including landlords, property managers and tenant screening companies.
minor_exemptions_not_in_data: Owner occupying a home and renting to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics (but may not publish discriminatory advertisements)

rules.exemptions: An owner occupying a home and renting to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but still cannot make, print or publish discriminatory statements, notices or advertisements.
rules.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
rules.quoted_span: California law protects tenants from discrimination based on how a tenant will be paying rent (“source of income”). This includes the State of California’s COVID-19 Rent Relief Program, Housing Choice (Section 8) vouchers, (SSI) social security disability benefits, or wages earned from a job.
rules.penalty: Remedies include out-of-pocket losses, injunctions, access to the denied housing, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney's fees.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of one month's rent (AB 12)
rules.requirement: Since July 1, 2024, most landlords may charge a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, whether or not the unit is furnished. Last month's rent counts toward the cap; first month's rent does not. Small landlords may charge up to two months' rent.
rules.key_value: 1 month rent (2 months for qualifying small landlords)

coverage_conditions.summary: Applies to residential rental units statewide, furnished or unfurnished. Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units in total may charge up to two months' rent. This applies only if the owner is a natural person, a family trust, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons.

rules.exemptions: Small landlords may charge up to two months' rent. They must own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total, held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC whose members are all natural persons.
rules.quoted_span: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units

rules.title: Security deposit cap of one month's rent
rules.requirement: Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member.
rules.key_value: 1 month rent (2 months for qualifying small landlords)

coverage_conditions.summary: All residential rental property used as the tenant's dwelling. Small individual landlords owning no more than two rental properties with four or fewer units in total may charge up to two months' rent, except to service members.

rules.title: Deposit return and itemized statement within 21 days; bad-faith penalty
rules.requirement: Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages.

rules.quoted_span: (m) The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section, or the bad faith demand of replacement of security in violation of subdivision (k), may subject the landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.
rules.penalty: Statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages, for bad faith claim or retention; landlord forfeits claim to security if it fails in bad faith to comply.

rules.title: No nonrefundable deposits
rules.requirement: A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.

rules.title: Only licensed brokers may charge fees for finding rental housing
rules.requirement: Only a licensed real estate broker or salesperson may charge a fee for finding an apartment for a prospective tenant. Do not pay a finder's fee to an unlicensed person.

rules.title: Broker fee paid only by the party who hired the broker
rules.requirement: In Massachusetts, a rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who originally hired and contracted with the broker. If the landlord hired the broker, you as a tenant cannot be made to pay that fee.

rules.title: Protection against retaliatory reprisal and eviction; six-month presumption
rules.requirement: A landlord who threatens or takes reprisals (including eviction notices, rent increases or changed lease terms) because you complained about code violations, took legal action, or joined a tenants' union owes you at least one to three months' rent or your actual damages plus attorney's fees. A termination notice (other than for nonpayment), rent increase or substantial change in terms within six months after such activity is presumed to be retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence.
rules.key_value: Damages 1-3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever greater; 6-month presumption

coverage_conditions.summary: All tenants of residential premises in Massachusetts.

rules.exemptions: Notices of termination for nonpayment of rent do not trigger the presumption.

rules.title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control (Rent Control Prohibition Act)
rules.requirement: Massachusetts cities and towns generally cannot enact, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no local rent cap to rely on. The only exception is a voluntary program for owners of 10 or more units with fair market rent of $400 or less, where the city pays owners the difference from its general funds.

rules.exemptions: A city or town that accepts chapter 40P may adopt rent control regulation only if all of the following hold: (a) owner compliance is entirely voluntary after six months; (b) it does not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties, and it does not apply to units of owners with fewer than ten rental units or units with fair market rent over $400; and (c) the municipality compensates owners for the gap between fair market rent and the controlled rent from general funds.
